column1: Built-in REGEXP_* functions were introduced in SQL Server {{c1::2025}}.
column2:
Earlier SQL Server versions do not provide these built-in regex functions.
Review source

column1: The regex quantifier {{c1::*}} means zero or more repetitions of the preceding expression.
column2:
For example, ab*c also matches ac.
Review source

column1: The regex quantifier {{c1::+}} means one or more repetitions of the preceding expression.
column2:
For example, ab+c requires at least one b.
Review source

column1: The regex quantifier {{c1::?}} makes the preceding expression optional.
column2:
It allows zero or one occurrence.
Review source

column1: With the m flag absent, the regex anchor {{c1::^}} requires the beginning of the input text.
column2:
Place it before the expression that must start the input.
Review source

column1: With the m flag absent, the regex anchor {{c1::$}} requires the end of the input text.
column2:
Place it after the expression that must end the input.
Review source

column1: The regex character class {{c1::[abc]}} matches one a, b, or c.
column2:
Square brackets define a set of allowed characters.
Review source

column1: The regex character class {{c1::[^0-9]}} matches one character that is not an ASCII digit.
column2:
A leading caret inside the brackets negates the class.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server regex, {{c1::\d}} is shorthand for [0-9].
column2:
This shorthand matches ASCII digits.
Review source

column1: Exactly four repetitions of the preceding regex expression use the quantifier {{c1::{4}}}.
column2:
The repetition count applies to the immediately preceding expression.
Review source

column1: Between two and four repetitions of the preceding regex expression use the quantifier {{c1::{2,4}}}.
column2:
Both the minimum and maximum counts are inclusive.
Review source

column1: The regex operator {{c1::|}} provides alternation, as in cat|dog.
column2:
The pattern can match either alternative.
Review source

column1: To match a literal period rather than a wildcard, use the regex pattern {{c1::\.}}.
column2:
A backslash escapes the period's special regex meaning.
Review source

column1: Capture a digit run with the regex group {{c1::(\d+)}}.
column2:
Parentheses create a numbered capture group.
Review source

column1: SQL Server regex uses flag {{c1::c}} for its default case-sensitive matching.
column2:
Case sensitivity is controlled by regex flags rather than SQL collation.
Review source

column1: Case-insensitive SQL Server regex matching uses flag {{c1::i}}.
column2:
For example, REGEXP_LIKE(Name,'frame','i') ignores letter case.
Review source

column1: SQL Server regex flag {{c1::s}} allows . to match a newline.
column2:
Without this flag, the dot excludes newline characters.
Review source

column1: SQL Server regex flag {{c1::m}} lets ^ and $ match line boundaries within multiline text.
column2:
The anchors can match line boundaries in addition to the input's boundaries.
Review source

column1: Swap Smith, John to John Smith with REGEXP_REPLACE('Smith, John','^(\w+),\s*(\w+)$',{{c1::'\2 \1'}}).
column2:
SQL Server replacement text uses \1 through \9 to reference captured groups.
Review source

column1: Collapse whitespace runs to one space with REGEXP_REPLACE(@s,{{c1::'\s+'}},' ').
column2:
The + matches one or more whitespace characters.
Review source

column1: Extract the second digit run with REGEXP_SUBSTR(@s,'\d+',1,{{c1::2}}).
column2:
The fourth argument selects the matching occurrence.
Review source

column1: Extract an email domain without @ using REGEXP_SUBSTR(@email,'@(.+)$',1,1,'c',{{c1::1}}).
column2:
Group 1 returns the text captured inside parentheses instead of the whole match.
Review source

column1: REGEXP_INSTR('AB12','\d') returns {{c1::3}}.
column2:
The first digit starts at the third character.
Review source

column1: Count digit runs in @s with {{c1::REGEXP_COUNT(@s,'\d+')}}.
column2:
Each run of consecutive digits contributes one match.
Review source

column1: Split on commas, semicolons, or pipes with REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE(@s,{{c1::'[,;|]'}}).
column2:
Inside this character class, the pipe is a literal delimiter.
Review source

column1: Return split tokens in input order with SELECT value FROM REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE(@s,',') {{c1::ORDER BY ordinal}}.
column2:
The ordinal column records each token's 1-based input position.
Review source
